# How can we get reliable information from images?

::: {.story-lead}
Images of seeds are both data for classifying plants and a test case for image
segmentation. This line of work has followed three connected threads:
separating seeds from the background, classifying seeds from their images and
validating segmentations with classifiers, up to PARSEG, which needs only a
small sample of pixels.
:::
:::

::: {.column-margin .glance}
**At a glance**

Period
:   2011 to 2024

Threads
:   Segmentation by background subtraction; classification of seeds; validation of segmentation

Selected collaborators
:   Jaromír Antoch, Claudio Conversano, Francesco Mola, Gianluigi
    Bacchetta. All authors are listed [with each publication](#publications).

Data
:   Images of botanical seeds

Key paper
:   *Scientific Reports* 2024 (open access)

Code
:   [R implementation on GitHub](https://github.com/lucafrigau/parseg)
:::

## The question

Image segmentation separates the objects of interest, such as seeds, from the
background, and many algorithms can do it. Images of seeds are also used to
measure their size, texture and shape and to classify them. But how do we know
that a segmentation is right, and how can we check it when an image has
millions of pixels?

## Where it started [2011–2016]{.period} {#origins}

The first works of this line date from the years of my joint PhD, in
Probability and Mathematical Statistics at Charles University in Prague and in
Environmental and Applied Botany at the University of Cagliari, which I
completed in 2016 with a thesis on morpho-colorimetric and non-parametric
analysis in the statistical classification of vascular flora.

In October 2011 I was a visiting fellow at the Department of Probability and
Mathematical Statistics of Charles University, to work on classification
methods based on Fourier analysis, a technique that
also appears in the study of *Prunus* seeds [described
below](#classification).

## Separating the seed from the background [2015–2016]{.period} {#background}

Segmentation algorithms separate the foreground from the background using
the intensity of the pixels, so it is good practice to choose a background
colour as different as possible from that of the objects. When many images are
digitized, it is useful to take this choice away from the user and automate
the process; moreover, high-resolution images slow down the algorithms based
on local thresholding.

We adapted background subtraction, a method used to detect moving objects in
videos, to image segmentation. It combines local and global thresholding,
gives good segmentations, automates the process when the colour of the objects is not
constant and speeds it up considerably; on images of botanical seeds, its
results were compared statistically with those of standard segmentation
methods ({{< cite mola2016classification >}}). Two conference contributions had
preceded the article ({{< cite frigau2015improving text="ISI 2015" >}};
{{< cite mola2015background text="ODAM 2015" >}}).

## Classifying seeds from their images [2018–2020]{.period} {#classification}

In taxonomic studies, digital image analysis is increasingly used to compare
and discriminate groups of seeds. A conference contribution compared
non-parametric approaches to the classification of seeds
({{< cite frigau2018comparison text="ISBIS 2018" >}}).

The many variables measured on seeds, on size, texture and shape, are
generally used in classification algorithms without any pre-processing, which
brings noise and makes the process less consistent for new samples. In a
study of 19 Sardinian cultivars of *Prunus domestica* and four cultivars of
other *Prunus* species, the variables of each kind were pre-processed
separately, with principal component analysis and Fourier analysis.

The accuracy of each kind of data was then measured by comparing k-nearest
neighbours, linear discriminant analysis, naive Bayes, support vector machines
and random forests. The combination of size, texture and shape discriminated
the seeds well, and image analysis with pre-processed data proved useful down
to the cultivar level ({{< cite frigau2020statistical >}}).

## Is the segmentation right? [2016–2021]{.period} {#validation}

A statistical approach to validation uses the labels that a segmentation
method assigns to the pixels, foreground or background, as the response of a
classifier that predicts them from the colour of each pixel: the better the
two agree, the better the segmentation method is ranked.

Conference contributions of those years dealt with evaluating an image
segmentation method ({{< cite frigau2016evaluating text="ISBIS 2016" >}}) and
validating the segmentation of images of botanical seeds
({{< cite frigau2016validating text="Statistische Woche 2016" >}};
{{< cite antoch2017validation text="CLADAG 2017" >}}); one proposed a
classification-based approach to validating segmentation algorithms
({{< cite frigau2019classification text="y-BIS 2019" >}}). In December 2017 I
visited Charles University again, to work on computationally efficient
non-parametric methods for validating statistical image segmentation.

We proposed MaLIV, a machine
learning approach that ranks the outputs of different gray-level thresholding
segmentation algorithms, taking into account both the computational
complexity of the validation and the robustness of its results. It uses
subsampling to find Fisher-consistent estimates of validity measures from a
sample of pixels of very small size, combined with one of three alternative
approaches: learning curves, asymptotic regression and convergence in
probability. The article presents experiments on the validation of five
images segmented with thirteen algorithms ({{< cite frigau2021consistent >}}).

## How many pixels are enough? [2024]{.period} {#parseg}

When an image has millions of pixels, validation becomes very demanding, both
in practice and in computing time. PARSEG, which we developed, rests on an
empirical finding: the results of validation obtained by
training a classifier on all the pixels of an image are consistent with those
obtained from much smaller random samples of pixels of a suitable size
({{< cite frigau2024parseg >}}). The procedure:

1. partitions the image into subsets of pixels of approximately equal size;
2. on one subset, finds the minimum size of a random sample of pixels that
   preserves the information needed for validation, by studying how the
   performance of the classifier changes with the sample size;
3. validates the remaining subsets using only samples of that size, and
   combines the results.

{{< story-figure files="assets/img/stories/parseg-1-image.svg,assets/img/stories/parseg-2-sample.svg,assets/img/stories/parseg-3-curve.svg" labels="1 · Image|2 · Partition and random sample|3 · Smallest sufficient sample" caption="Schematic illustration with simulated data. In the second panel, dashed lines partition the segmented image and circles are randomly sampled pixels; in the third, the vertical line marks the smallest sample size at which the classifier's performance stabilizes." >}}

On images of seeds of about 13 million pixels, PARSEG gives roughly the same
precision as validation on the entire image.

::: {.big-numbers}

:::: {.big-number .big-number--accent}
[about 4%]{.big-number__value}
[of the pixels are used]{.big-number__label}
::::

:::: {.big-number .big-number--accent}
[about 90%]{.big-number__value}
[less computing time]{.big-number__label}
::::

:::

::: {.big-numbers-note}
Values reported in the abstract of the article, for the validation of a binary
segmented image.
:::
